Good morning, and thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today. As Zoe mentioned, last week I returned from Venezuela, where I've visited the communities hardest hit by the twin earthquakes, including La Guaira, the area most severely affected. I met families who lost everything, local authorities, humanitarian partners, and IOM staff working around the clock to support the response. Today marks one month after these devastating earthquakes. It has been a month of immense immense loss, grief, and uncertainty. But it has also been a month of extraordinary courage and bravery. As I went through the affected neighborhoods, I was struck by the scale of the destruction, but even more, the strength and solidarity of the people I met. I witnessed entire communities pulling together to help, including those affected by the earthquakes. Families shared heartbreaking stories of losing loved ones, their homes, their belongings, and their livelihoods in a matter of seconds. Many are still living next to the collapsed and/or heavily damaged buildings, hoping that loved ones can still be recovered or trying to salvage the few possessions they have left. The emotional toll is enormous. People are living with trauma, anxiety, and uncertainty about what comes next. Children, parents, and older people alike need not only shelter and basic assistance, but also continued psychosocial support to help them begin to recover. Across these affected areas, one message came through very clearly: people need a safe place to live. Shelter remains the most urgent priority. A safe place to live is much more than a roof overhead. It's the foundation for recovery. Without safe shelter, it is impossible to restore any sort of normal life, for children to return to school, for parents to return to work, and for a sense of stability to be reestablished. Many families Families continue to move between temporary shelters, staying with relatives or wherever they can find space. Understanding where people are moving is essential so that assistance reaches those who are in need. Protection risks are also increasing in some displacement sites as overcrowding, inadequate lighting, and limited communal spaces increase the risks of gender-based violence and human trafficking, particularly for women and girls. IOM is working side by side with the government of Venezuela and humanitarian partners to respond. We are managing 5 temporary shelters hosting around 6,000 people. So far, we have reached more than 8,200 people with shelter assistance, site coordination, healthcare, protection services, and displacement tracking. But we also know that recovery must begin now. Experience from emergencies around the world tell us that people cannot wait for the crisis to end before we build— start rebuilding their lives. To support this effort, IOM is appealing for $98 million to assist 850,000 people through a response that combines flight life-saving assistance with early recovery, resilience, and long-term solutions. This includes shelter, water and sanitation, protection, livelihoods, psychosocial support, and displacement tracking. The people of Venezuela have demonstrated incredible, incredible strength in the face of great loss. Our responsibility now is to stand with them not only in the immediate aftermath of the disaster, but throughout the long road to recovery. They need our support to heal and rebuild their homes and restore their communities. IOM calls on our partners to continue to give hope to Venezuela in their moment of greatest need.

Overall, 3 rescue and disembarkation operations were conducted between the 14th and the 18th of July in Nouadhibou, Mauritania. And that brought 387 people safely ashore. Another death was reported from among passengers on a boat that was disembarked on the 14th of July. Overall, this is a stark reminder that despite sustained efforts by coastal authorities and partners to save lives, the Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands remains one of the world's deadliest mixed movement corridors due to long distances, unpredictable ocean conditions, Unseaworthy and overcrowded boats, and limited access to timely rescue. Despite the number of arrivals to the Spanish archipelago dropping this year by some 61% from 2025, with 4,400 arrivals as of the 15th of July, the incidents do highlight the persistent risks faced by refugees and migrants attempting to reach Europe, many of whom were embarking from over 2,000 kilometres away from their intended destinations. Overall, if we look at arrivals to Europe by sea so far this year on the major routes, there have been over 40,000 this year compared to over 65,000 in the first half of 2025. Still, UNHCR and our partners have repeatedly warned that deaths and disappearances at sea continue at alarming levels, with many incidents occurring far from public attention and often resulting in entire boats vanishing. Against this backdrop, the rescues in Mauritania demonstrate that concerted efforts need to be made to address the root causes driving refugees and migrants to take these perilous journeys while providing quicker and meaningful access to legal pathways through which refugees and migrants can find safety and opportunity.
